claim: Uveal melanoma (UM) is a rare melanoma originating in the eye's uvea.
source: Uveal melanoma (UM) is a rare melanoma originating in the eye's uvea, with 50% of patients experiencing metastasis predominantly in the liver.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about uveal melanoma presented in the abstract.

claim: 50% of patients with uveal melanoma experience metastasis predominantly in the liver.
source: Uveal melanoma (UM) is a rare melanoma originating in the eye's uvea, with 50% of patients experiencing metastasis predominantly in the liver.
evidence: This is a statistical claim about metastasis rates in UM patients presented in the abstract.

claim: Combined immune checkpoint therapies have limited effectiveness in uveal melanoma compared to cutaneous melanoma.
source: In contrast to cutaneous melanoma, there is only a limited effectiveness of combined immune checkpoint therapies, and half of patients with uveal melanoma metastases succumb to disease within 2 years.
evidence: This claim compares treatment effectiveness between UM and cutaneous melanoma, drawing on established clinical knowledge.

claim: Half of patients with uveal melanoma metastases die within 2 years.
source: In contrast to cutaneous melanoma, there is only a limited effectiveness of combined immune checkpoint therapies, and half of patients with uveal melanoma metastases succumb to disease within 2 years.
evidence: This is a survival statistic for UM metastasis patients presented in the abstract.

claim: The study employed single-cell RNA-seq of biopsies and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to identify potential tumor-reactive T cells.
source: We employed single-cell RNA-seq of biopsies and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to identify potential tumor-reactive T cells.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: Patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models of UM metastases were created from patients.
source: Patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models of UM metastases were created from patients, and tumor sphere cultures were generated from these models for co-culture with autologous or MART1-specific HLA-matched allogenic TILs.
evidence: This describes the generation of PDX models as a method used in the study.

claim: Tumor sphere cultures were generated from PDX models for co-culture with autologous or MART1-specific HLA-matched allogenic TILs.
source: Patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models of UM metastases were created from patients, and tumor sphere cultures were generated from these models for co-culture with autologous or MART1-specific HLA-matched allogenic TILs.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach using tumor spheres and TILs.

claim: Activated T cells were subjected to TCR-seq and matched to those found in single-cell sequencing data from biopsies, expanded TILs, and in livers or spleens of PDX models injected with TILs.
source: Activated T cells were subjected to TCR-seq, and the TCRs were matched to those found in single-cell sequencing data from biopsies, expanded TILs, and in livers or spleens of PDX models injected with TILs.
evidence: This describes the TCR sequencing and matching methodology used in the study.

claim: Tumor-reactive T cells resided not only among activated and exhausted subsets of T cells, but also in a subset of cytotoxic effector cells.
source: Our findings revealed that tumor-reactive T cells resided not only among activated and exhausted subsets of T cells, but also in a subset of cytotoxic effector cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study regarding the phenotypic distribution of tumor-reactive T cells.

claim: Uveal melanoma develops in the uvea of the eye, most often in the choroid and ciliary body, and more infrequently in the iris.
source: It develops in the uvea of the eye, most often in the choroid and ciliary body, and more infrequently in the iris.
evidence: This is an anatomical description of where UM develops, based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Primary UM can be cured by brachytherapy or enucleation of the eye.
source: Primary UM can be cured by brachytherapy or enucleation of the eye, but 50% of patients will develop metastasis (Buder et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes treatment options for primary UM, supported by a citation.

claim: 50% of patients with primary UM will develop metastasis.
source: Primary UM can be cured by brachytherapy or enucleation of the eye, but 50% of patients will develop metastasis (Buder et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statistical claim about metastasis rates supported by a citation.

claim: The most common route for metastatic spread of UM is the liver.
source: The most common route for metastatic spread is the liver for reasons that are poorly understood.
evidence: This describes the metastatic pattern of UM based on clinical observations.

claim: The reasons for liver-predominant metastasis in UM are poorly understood.
source: The most common route for metastatic spread is the liver for reasons that are poorly understood.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in understanding about UM metastasis patterns.

claim: Patients with metastatic UM have a median survival of less than a year.
source: Patients with metastatic disease have a median survival of less than a year (Khoja et al., 2019) however, ongoing clinical studies suggest that some treatments could prolong survival (Carvajal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a survival statistic for metastatic UM patients supported by a citation.

claim: Ongoing clinical studies suggest that some treatments could prolong survival in metastatic UM.
source: Patients with metastatic disease have a median survival of less than a year (Khoja et al., 2019) however, ongoing clinical studies suggest that some treatments could prolong survival (Carvajal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about potential treatment benefits supported by a citation.

claim: Monotherapy immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) are markedly less effective in patients with UM than in those with metastatic cutaneous melanomas.
source: Monotherapy immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) are markedly less effective in patients with UM (Johnson et al., 2019; Algazi et al., 2016) than in those with metastatic cutaneous melanomas.
evidence: This compares ICI effectiveness between UM and cutaneous melanoma, supported by citations.

claim: Combination treatments with PD-1/CTLA-4 inhibitors have demonstrated longer overall survival than historic benchmark data in UM.
source: However, combination treatments with PD-1/CTLA-4 inhibitors (Piulats et al., 2021; Pelster et al., 2021; Najjar et al., 2020) or PD-1/HDAC inhibitors (Jespersen et al., 2019; Ny et al., 2021) have demonstrated longer overall survival than historic benchmark data (Khoja et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes treatment outcomes for combination therapies supported by multiple citations.

claim: Combination treatments with PD-1/HDAC inhibitors have demonstrated longer overall survival than historic benchmark data in UM.
source: However, combination treatments with PD-1/CTLA-4 inhibitors (Piulats et al., 2021; Pelster et al., 2021; Najjar et al., 2020) or PD-1/HDAC inhibitors (Jespersen et al., 2019; Ny et al., 2021) have demonstrated longer overall survival than historic benchmark data (Khoja et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes treatment outcomes for combination therapies supported by multiple citations.

claim: Tebentafusp is a T cell engager suitable for patients with the HLA-A2 genotype.
source: Tebentafusp, a T cell engager suitable for patients with the HLA-A2 genotype (Damato et al., 2019; Middleton et al., 2020), is the first therapy to show a prolonged overall survival in a phase 3 randomized trial, increasing median survival from 16.0 months to 21.7 months (Nathan et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of tebentafusp supported by citations.

claim: Tebentafusp is the first therapy to show a prolonged overall survival in a phase 3 randomized trial for UM, increasing median survival from 16.0 months to 21.7 months.
source: Tebentafusp, a T cell engager suitable for patients with the HLA-A2 genotype (Damato et al., 2019; Middleton et al., 2020), is the first therapy to show a prolonged overall survival in a phase 3 randomized trial, increasing median survival from 16.0 months to 21.7 months (Nathan et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes clinical trial results for tebentafusp supported by a citation.

claim: A recent phase 3 trial demonstrated that isolated hepatic perfusion (IHP) triples hepatic progression-free survival compared with the best alternative care and historic benchmark data.
source: Another development is locoregional treatments, where a recent phase 3 trial demonstrated that isolated hepatic perfusion (IHP) triples hepatic progression-free survival (Olofsson Bagge et al., 2023) compared with the best alternative care and historic benchmark data.
evidence: This describes clinical trial results for IHP supported by a citation.

claim: Retrospective data suggest an overall survival benefit with liver-directed therapy in UM.
source: Although retrospective data suggest an overall survival benefit with liver-directed therapy (Ben-Shabat et al., 2016), in the SCANDIUM phase 3 trial, overall survival of patients treated with IHP was not statistically significantly better that for patients treated with best alternative care (Olofsson Bagge et al., 2024).
evidence: This describes retrospective findings about liver-directed therapy supported by a citation.

claim: In the SCANDIUM phase 3 trial, overall survival of patients treated with IHP was not statistically significantly better than for patients treated with best alternative care.
source: Although retrospective data suggest an overall survival benefit with liver-directed therapy (Ben-Shabat et al., 2016), in the SCANDIUM phase 3 trial, overall survival of patients treated with IHP was not statistically significantly better that for patients treated with best alternative care (Olofsson Bagge et al., 2024).
evidence: This describes clinical trial results for IHP supported by a citation.

claim: All patients progressed on both tebentafusp and IHP.
source: Moreover, invariably, all patients progressed on both tebentafusp and IHP; therefore, more research is needed.
evidence: This describes treatment outcomes indicating eventual disease progression.

claim: Pilot data from a clinical trial showed that TILs can cause responses in patients with UM.
source: Pilot data from a clinical trial (Chandran et al., 2017) showed that TILs can cause responses in patients, and we have previously showed that HER2 CAR-T cells can eradicate UM in xenografts (Forsberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes clinical trial results for TIL therapy supported by a citation.

claim: HER2 CAR-T cells can eradicate UM in xenografts.
source: Pilot data from a clinical trial (Chandran et al., 2017) showed that TILs can cause responses in patients, and we have previously showed that HER2 CAR-T cells can eradicate UM in xenografts (Forsberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes previous experimental findings by the authors supported by a citation.

claim: There is a lack of robust ex vivo screening models for UM.
source: There is, however, a lack of robust ex vivo screening models and very few patient-derived xenograft (PDX) mouse models from metastases (Carita et al., 2015) to use in studies to improve ACT.
evidence: This identifies a gap in available research tools for UM.

claim: There are very few patient-derived xenograft (PDX) mouse models from UM metastases.
source: There is, however, a lack of robust ex vivo screening models and very few patient-derived xenograft (PDX) mouse models from metastases (Carita et al., 2015) to use in studies to improve ACT.
evidence: This identifies a limitation in available research models supported by a citation.

claim: UM has lower mutation burden compared to cutaneous melanoma.
source: Part of the lack of success for ACT may be attributable to a lack of tumor-reactive lymphocytes, possibly owing to lower mutation burden in UM compared to cutaneous melanoma (van der Kooij et al., 2019).
evidence: This compares mutation burden between UM and cutaneous melanoma supported by a citation.

claim: The lower mutation burden in UM may contribute to a lack of tumor-reactive lymphocytes.
source: Part of the lack of success for ACT may be attributable to a lack of tumor-reactive lymphocytes, possibly owing to lower mutation burden in UM compared to cutaneous melanoma (van der Kooij et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between mutation burden and tumor-reactive lymphocytes.

claim: Clinical trial and previous analyses of TILs in UM liver metastases have suggested that at least some TILs are tumor reactive.
source: However, both the clinical trial and previous analyses of TILs in UM liver metastases have suggested that at least some TILs are tumor reactive (Chandran et al., 2017; Durante et al., 2020; Karlsson et al., 2020; Rothermel et al., 2016).
evidence: This summarizes findings from multiple studies supported by citations.

claim: The study obtained biopsies suitable for sequencing from 14 patients, two of which were subcutaneous and 12 were liver metastases.
source: We obtained biopsies suitable for sequencing from 14 patients, two of which were subcutaneous and 12 were liver metastases.
evidence: This describes the sample composition used in the study.

claim: The study created the largest single-cell atlas of metastatic UM to date.
source: This has resulted in the largest single-cell atlas of metastatic UM to date, complementing prior efforts, including our own study of TILs from UM metastases (Durante et al., 2020; Karlsson et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2021; Pandiani et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the scope of the dataset generated in the study.

claim: UMAP dimensionality-reduced expression profiles revealed clusters containing melanoma, CD8+ or CD4+ T cells, NK cells, monocytes, and small clusters of B cells, endothelial cells, and other minor cell populations.
source: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) dimensionality-reduced expression profiles revealed clusters containing melanoma, CD8+ or CD4+ T cells, NK cells, monocytes, and small clusters of B cells, endothelial cells, and other minor cell populations (Figure 1b and c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–f).
evidence: This describes the cell types identified through single-cell analysis, supported by figures.

claim: Clusters were generally well mixed with respect to contributions from different samples, suggesting few patient-specific or batch effects after data integration.
source: Clusters were generally well mixed with respect to contributions from different samples, suggesting few patient-specific or batch effects after data integration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This describes the quality of data integration based on analysis of sample contributions.

claim: The identity of cells labeled as UM was confirmed by inferring copy number changes that revealed characteristic aberrations seen in metastatic UM, including monosomy of chromosome 3 and gain of 8q.
source: The identity of cells labeled as UM was further confirmed by inferring copy number changes. This revealed characteristic aberrations seen in metastatic UM, including monosomy of chromosome 3 and gain of 8q, as well as subclonal variation within patients (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This describes validation of UM cell identity through copy number analysis.

claim: Subclustering of CD8+ T cells showed the presence of 12 different groups.
source: Further subclustering of CD8+ T cells showed the presence of 12 different groups (Figure 2a and b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1i–k), all characterized by the differential expression of immunological marker genes (Figure 2c and d and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the results of CD8+ T cell subclustering analysis.

claim: CD8+ T cell clusters can be divided into two axes, one characterized by expression of genes associated with late activation and exhaustion.
source: The clusters can be divided into two axes. One of these is characterized by expression of genes associated with late activation and exhaustion, such as PDCD1, HAVCR2, TNFRSF9, and HLA-DRA.
evidence: This describes the phenotypic organization of CD8+ T cell clusters.

claim: Expression of ITGAE (CD103) suggests that exhausted CD8+ T cell clusters contain tissue-resident memory cells.
source: Additional expression of ITGAE (CD103) suggests that these clusters contain tissue-resident memory cells (Ganesan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of gene expression data supported by a citation.

claim: Multiplex immunofluorescence showed that PD-1- and ICOS-expressing T cells were in close proximity to the tumor cells.
source: Multiplex immunofluorescence showed that PD-1- and ICOS-expressing T cells were in close proximity to the tumor cells (Figure 2e).
evidence: This describes spatial relationships observed through immunofluorescence imaging.

claim: The other axis of CD8+ T cells expressed genes associated with naïve/memory-like or early activated phenotypes, such as IL7R, TCF7, CCR7, and NR4A1.
source: The other axis expressed genes associated with naïve/memory-like or early activated phenotypes, such as IL7R, TCF7, CCR7, and NR4A1 (Figure 2d).
evidence: This describes the phenotypic characteristics of the second axis of CD8+ T cells.

claim: One CD8+ T cell cluster expressed KLRB1 and NCR3.
source: Two of these were within the IL7+ axis. Of these, one expressed KLRB1 and NCR3 and the other expressed NK-associated markers, such as FCGR3A, FCRL6, and NKG7 (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This describes marker expression in a specific CD8+ T cell cluster.

claim: One CD8+ T cell cluster expressed NK-associated markers, such as FCGR3A, FCRL6, and NKG7.
source: Two of these were within the IL7+ axis. Of these, one expressed KLRB1 and NCR3 and the other expressed NK-associated markers, such as FCGR3A, FCRL6, and NKG7 (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This describes marker expression in a specific CD8+ T cell cluster.

claim: Only the NK-associated CD8+ T cell cluster expressed GZMB and GZMH.
source: Although both clusters expressed genes related to cytotoxicity, only the latter expressed GZMB and GZMH.
evidence: This describes differential expression of cytotoxic markers between clusters.

claim: The NK-associated CD8+ T cell cluster is associated with markers CX3CR1 and FGFBP2.
source: Other markers associated with this group are CX3CR1 and FGFBP2.
evidence: This describes additional markers for the NK-associated CD8+ T cell cluster.

claim: Previous studies labeled NK-associated CD8+ T cells as cytotoxic NK-like T cells.
source: Previous studies labeled these cells as cytotoxic NK-like T cells (Li et al., 2019; Huuhtanen, 2023).
evidence: This references prior characterization of similar cell types supported by citations.

claim: The initial take rate of PDX models using single-cell dispersion method was unsatisfactory for UM.
source: However, the biopsies we received were generally very small, and the initial take rate using the same single-cell dispersion method used for cutaneous melanoma metastases (Patton et al., 2021) was unsatisfactory.
evidence: This describes challenges in establishing PDX models for UM.

claim: Transplanting small tumor pieces or using splenic injections led to successful PDX generation for some patients.
source: Therefore, we transplanted small tumor pieces or used splenic injections, which led to successful PDX generation for some patients.
evidence: This describes the modified approach that improved PDX generation success.

claim: Ten PDX models are presented in this study.
source: Ten of these are presented in this study.
evidence: This states the number of PDX models included in the study.

claim: All the PDX tumors exhibited confirmatory markers of melanoma, such as SOX10, MELAN-A (MART1), HMB45, or S100B.
source: All the PDX tumors exhibited confirmatory markers of melanoma, such as SOX10, MELAN-A (MART1), HMB45, or S100B.
evidence: This describes validation of PDX tumor identity through marker expression.

claim: Sanger sequencing revealed mutually exclusive mutations in the UM oncogenes GNAQ, GNA11, CYSLTR2, and PLCB4 in PDX models, as found in biopsies.
source: Sanger sequencing further revealed mutually exclusive mutations in the UM oncogenes GNAQ, GNA11, CYSLTR2, and PLCB4, as found in biopsies (Karlsson et al., 2020; Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes genetic validation of PDX models through sequencing.

claim: UM tumors grew at a slower rate compared to cutaneous melanoma in PDX models.
source: The UM tumors grew at a slower rate compared to our experience with cutaneous melanoma, which has a take rate of 95% and where a model is usually established within 3–12 weeks (Figure 3b; Einarsdottir et al., 2014).
evidence: This compares growth rates between UM and cutaneous melanoma PDX models.

claim: Cutaneous melanoma PDX models have a take rate of 95% and are usually established within 3–12 weeks.
source: The UM tumors grew at a slower rate compared to our experience with cutaneous melanoma, which has a take rate of 95% and where a model is usually established within 3–12 weeks (Figure 3b; Einarsdottir et al., 2014).
evidence: This provides comparative data on cutaneous melanoma PDX models supported by a citation.

claim: Injection of autologous TILs into hIL2-NOG mice carrying UM1 resulted in tumor rejection.
source: The injection of autologous TILs into hIL2-NOG mice carrying UM1 resulted in tumor rejection, whereas UM22 tumors could not be eradicated (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This describes experimental results of TIL therapy in a PDX model.

claim: UM22 tumors could not be eradicated by autologous TILs in hIL2-NOG mice.
source: The injection of autologous TILs into hIL2-NOG mice carrying UM1 resulted in tumor rejection, whereas UM22 tumors could not be eradicated (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This describes experimental results showing lack of tumor eradication in one PDX model.

claim: TILs from UM metastases can kill autologous tumors in a PDXv2 model.
source: This constitutes proof of concept that TILs from UM metastases can kill autologous tumors in a PDXv2 model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with UM1.

claim: The study generated tumor sphere cultures from 10 PDX models.
source: We generated tumor sphere cultures from 10 PDX models and expanded their autologous TILs (Figure 3e).
evidence: This describes the generation of tumor sphere cultures for experiments.

claim: TILs from patients UM1 and UM9 were activated the most (surface 4-1BB+) when co-cultured with tumor spheres.
source: When tumor spheres and TILs were co-cultured, TILs from patients UM1 and UM9 were activated the most (surface 4-1BB+) and also degranulated (surface CD107a+; Figure 3f and g).
evidence: This describes experimental results of TIL activation in co-culture assays.

claim: TILs from patients UM1 and UM9 degranulated (surface CD107a+) when co-cultured with tumor spheres.
source: When tumor spheres and TILs were co-cultured, TILs from patients UM1 and UM9 were activated the most (surface 4-1BB+) and also degranulated (surface CD107a+; Figure 3f and g).
evidence: This describes experimental results of TIL degranulation in co-culture assays.

claim: TILs from UM1 and UM9 bound to tumor spheres, as assessed by labeling with different vital dyes and imaging.
source: These TILs also bound to the tumor spheres, as assessed by labeling tumor spheres and TILs with different vital dyes and then imaging with a real-time cell culture imager (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes experimental observation of TIL-tumor sphere binding.

claim: UM22 TILs were hardly able to get activated by their autologous tumor spheres.
source: The UM22 TILs were hardly able to get activated by their autologous tumor spheres (Figure 3b), which likely explains their lack of activity in the PDX ACT experiment (Figure 3d).
evidence: This describes experimental results and provides an interpretation for lack of activity.

claim: UM22 is capable of presenting MART1 on HLA-A2.
source: However, since UM22 is capable of presenting MART1 on HLA-A2, and since we previously identified a minor population of MART1-reactive TILs in this biopsy (Karlsson et al., 2020), we decided to expand and enrich this subset using MART1 peptide HLA-A2 dextramers.
evidence: This describes antigen presentation capability of UM22 tumors.

claim: A minor population of MART1-reactive TILs was previously identified in the UM22 biopsy.
source: However, since UM22 is capable of presenting MART1 on HLA-A2, and since we previously identified a minor population of MART1-reactive TILs in this biopsy (Karlsson et al., 2020), we decided to expand and enrich this subset using MART1 peptide HLA-A2 dextramers.
evidence: This references previous findings by the authors supported by a citation.

claim: MART1-enriched UM22 TILs achieved potent activation and degranulation when co-cultured with tumor spheres.
source: When using these cells, we were able to achieve potent activation and degranulation (Figure 3f and g).
evidence: This describes experimental results with MART1-enriched TILs.

claim: T cells extracted from biopsies can contain subsets capable of recognizing and killing tumors, which can be expanded ex vivo.
source: This confirms that T cells extracted from biopsies can contain subsets capable of recognizing and killing tumors, which can be expanded ex vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with MART1-enriched TILs.

claim: Tumor-reactive lymphocytes from UM1 and UM9 predominantly emanated from exhausted and late-activated cells.
source: This showed that those TRLs predominantly emanated from exhausted and late-activated cells (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This describes the phenotypic origin of TRLs identified through TCR mapping.

claim: UM9 contained a sizeable amount of TRLs in the NK-like/cytolytic cluster.
source: UM9 also contained a sizeable amount of TRLs in the NK-like/cytolytic cluster (Figure 4b).
evidence: This describes the distribution of TRLs in UM9 based on TCR mapping.

claim: The lack of potential TRL clones identified in the TCF7+ axis of the CD8+ T cell atlas from biopsies is compatible with a previous report showing that TCF7+ T cells in melanoma tend to be non-reactive bystanders.
source: The lack of potential TRL clones identified in the TCF7+ axis of the CD8+ T cell atlas from biopsies is also compatible with a previous report showing that TCF7+ T cells in melanoma tend to be non-reactive bystanders (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This interprets the absence of TRLs in certain clusters based on prior literature.

claim: Cells from the TIL dataset tended to correspond to biopsy T cells with exhausted and late-activated profiles.
source: Cells from the TIL dataset tended to correspond to biopsy T cells with exhausted and late-activated profiles, similar to the experimentally identified TRLs.
evidence: This describes the phenotypic correspondence between TIL cultures and biopsy T cells.

claim: TRLs were significantly overrepresented in proliferative exhausted and IL7R+ exhausted T cell clusters compared to TILs in general.
source: However, TRLs were significantly over- and underrepresented in some phenotypic clusters compared to TILs in general. Overrepresented clusters included proliferative exhausted and IL7R+ exhausted T cells.
evidence: This describes statistical analysis of TRL distribution across clusters.

claim: TRLs were significantly underrepresented in activated (non-exhausted), naïve/memory-like, and FCGR3A+ NK-like T cell clusters compared to TILs in general.
source: The underrepresented ones were activated (non-exhausted), naïve/memory-like, and FCGR3A+ NK-like T cells.
evidence: This describes statistical analysis of TRL distribution across clusters.

claim: The distribution of TRLs across clusters was different for cells sorted by 4-1BB positivity versus MART1 recognition.
source: The distribution of TRLs across the clusters was also different for cells sorted by 4-1BB positivity versus MART1 recognition.
evidence: This describes differences in TRL distribution based on selection method.

claim: MART1-reactive cells were more likely to be found in exhausted and late-activated clusters than 4-1BB+ cells.
source: MART1-reactive cells were more likely to be found in exhausted and late-activated clusters than 4-1BB+ cells, which tended to map to earlier activation states as well to the NK-like cluster (Figure 4e).
evidence: This describes differential distribution of TRLs based on selection method.

claim: 4-1BB+ cells tended to map to earlier activation states as well as to the NK-like cluster.
source: MART1-reactive cells were more likely to be found in exhausted and late-activated clusters than 4-1BB+ cells, which tended to map to earlier activation states as well to the NK-like cluster (Figure 4e).
evidence: This describes the distribution of 4-1BB+ TRLs across clusters.

claim: A large fraction of TILs in UM1 and UM9 cultures were among the identified TRL clones.
source: Mapping TCRs from enriched 4-1BB+ cells to TILs in corresponding patients from previously published TCR-seq data revealed that a large fraction of TILs in these cultures was among the identified TRL clones (Figure 4f).
evidence: This describes the overlap between TRL clones and TIL cultures.

claim: Five of six TIL cultures had many TCRs that overlapped between TILs and biopsies.
source: In six of the eight previously published TIL cultures, we were able to recover and sequence the corresponding cryopreserved biopsy of that patient. Five of the six cultures had many TCRs that overlapped between TILs and biopsies (Figure 4g and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This describes the degree of TCR overlap between TILs and biopsies.

claim: UM3 did not have any matching TCRs between the biopsies and expanded TIL cultures.
source: UM3 did not have any matching TCRs between the biopsies and expanded TIL cultures.
evidence: This describes an exception in TCR overlap between biopsies and TIL cultures.

claim: No overlap was observed between samples from different patients with the 4-1BB+/MART1+-selected TCRs.
source: No overlap was observed between samples from different patients with the 4-1BB+/MART1+-selected TCRs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This describes the patient-specificity of identified TRL TCRs.

claim: Very few clonotypes were shared between samples from different patients.
source: In general, very few clonotypes were shared between samples from different patients (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This describes the patient-specificity of TCR repertoires.

claim: A number of TCRs matched known MART1-reactive clonotypes in public databases.
source: The results confirmed that a number of TCRs matched known MART1-reactive clonotypes but also revealed matching TCRs that might recognize other melanoma antigens, such as PMEL and MAGEA1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f, g, and h).
evidence: This describes results of matching TCRs to public databases.

claim: Some TCRs matched clonotypes that might recognize melanoma antigens such as PMEL and MAGEA1.
source: The results confirmed that a number of TCRs matched known MART1-reactive clonotypes but also revealed matching TCRs that might recognize other melanoma antigens, such as PMEL and MAGEA1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f, g, and h).
evidence: This describes potential antigen recognition by identified TCRs based on database matches.

claim: A large number of TCRs matched clonotypes recognizing viral antigens such as influenza, EBV, and human coronaviruses.
source: Overall, a large number of TCRs also matched clonotypes recognizing viral antigens such as influenza, EBV, and human coronaviruses.
evidence: This describes results of matching TCRs to viral antigen databases.

claim: An even greater number of TCRs lacked known matches in public databases, suggesting they might recognize tumor-specific antigens (neoantigens).
source: However, an even greater number lacked known matches, suggesting they might recognize tumor-specific antigens (neoantigens).
evidence: This is an inference about potential neoantigen recognition based on lack of database matches.

claim: GLIPH2 nominated a few high-confidence clusters of similar TCR sequences based on the biopsy scRNA-seq data.
source: GLIPH2 (Huang et al., 2020) nominated a few high-confidence clusters of similar TCR sequences based on the biopsy scRNA-seq data (Figure 4h and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes results of computational TCR clustering analysis.

claim: The highest-ranked GLIPH2 cluster was overrepresented for sequences matching MART1 and exhibited significant restriction toward HLA-A*02:01.
source: Interestingly, the highest-ranked cluster was overrepresented for sequences matching MART1, and this cluster also exhibited significant restriction toward HLA-A*02:01, on which MART1 is known to be presented.
evidence: This describes characteristics of a computationally identified TCR cluster.

claim: The bioinformatically determined cluster of potential MART1-recognizing clones mostly belonged to the exhausted CD8+ T cell cluster.
source: Similar to the experimentally determined MART1-reactive T cells, the bioinformatically determined cluster of potential MART1-recognizing clones mostly belonged to the exhausted CD8+ T cell cluster (Figure 4i, Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This describes the phenotypic distribution of computationally predicted MART1-reactive cells.

claim: A high-confidence group of clonotypes co-localized to the NK-like cluster was nominated by GLIPH2, although no sequences from this cluster matched public TCR-antigen pairs.
source: In addition, a high-confidence group of clonotypes co-localized to the NK-like cluster was nominated by GLIPH2, although no sequences from this cluster matched the public TCR-antigen pairs (Figure 4h, Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This describes a computationally identified TCR cluster without known antigen matches.

claim: Cells from the NK-like cluster with high-confidence GLIPH2 clonotypes were experimentally identified as 4-1BB+ upon tumor co-culture.
source: Given that the cells from this cluster were experimentally identified as 4-1BB+ upon tumor co-culture (Figure 4b), one might speculate that they could recognize unknown tumor antigens.
evidence: This connects computational predictions with experimental validation.

claim: NK-like cluster cells with high-confidence GLIPH2 clonotypes might recognize unknown tumor antigens.
source: Given that the cells from this cluster were experimentally identified as 4-1BB+ upon tumor co-culture (Figure 4b), one might speculate that they could recognize unknown tumor antigens.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential antigen recognition based on experimental and computational data.

claim: Bioinformatically inferred TRLs from biopsies and ex vivo expanded TRLs tend to have exhausted phenotypes.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that both bioinformatically inferred TRLs from biopsies and ex vivo expanded TRLs tend to have exhausted phenotypes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Among exhausted TRLs, T cells recognize known melanoma antigens such as MART1, PMEL, and MAGEA1, as well as unknown sequences that might be neoantigens.
source: Among these, T cells recognize known melanoma antigens such as MART1, PMEL, and MAGEA1, as well as unknown sequences that might be neoantigens.
evidence: This summarizes the antigen recognition patterns of identified TRLs.

claim: MART1-selected TILs had a higher degree of activation than unselected bulk UM22 TILs in the liver metastasis PDX model.
source: As expected from Figure 3f and g, MART1-selected TILs had a higher degree of activation than unselected bulk UM22 TILs (Figure 5b), despite similar numbers of TILs present in the livers.
evidence: This describes experimental results comparing MART1-selected and bulk TILs in vivo.

claim: There were no visible differences in the size of liver tumors between mice receiving unselected or MART1-selected UM22 TILs.
source: There were no visible differences in the size of the liver tumors between mice receiving unselected or MART1-selected UM22 TILs.
evidence: This describes tumor size measurements in the PDX experiment.

claim: Most TILs colonized the rim of the tumor in the UM22 liver metastasis model, which may be due to T cell exclusion.
source: This may be due to T cell exclusion, since most TILs colonized the rim of the tumor (Figure 5c).
evidence: This describes spatial distribution of TILs and provides an interpretation.

claim: More MART1-specific TILs than unselected TILs were able to get activated, as assessed by the activation markers 4-1BB and CD69.
source: More MART1-specific TILs than unselected TILs were able to get activated, as assessed by the activation markers 4-1BB and CD69 (Figure 5b, d, and e).
evidence: This describes experimental results comparing activation of MART1-selected and bulk TILs.

claim: T cells recognizing a tumor antigen can successfully migrate to liver metastases of UM in mice.
source: This shows that T cells recognizing a tumor antigen can successfully migrate to liver metastases of UM in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MART1-selected TIL migration experiment.

claim: CD8+ T cells in PDX samples did not separate with respect to the same set of markers as in biopsies.
source: Compared with CD8+ T cell clusters from the biopsies, the clusters found in mice did not separate with respect to the same set of markers.
evidence: This describes differences in CD8+ T cell phenotypes between biopsies and PDX samples.

claim: All CD8+ T cell clusters in PDX samples expressed markers compatible with late-activated or exhausted cytotoxic cells to some extent.
source: Rather, all clusters expressed markers compatible with late-activated or exhausted cytotoxic cells to some extent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This describes the phenotypic characteristics of CD8+ T cells in PDX samples.

claim: There was a notable correspondence between liver TILs and C1, and between spleen TILs and C2 in the PDX samples.
source: These TILs were detectable in both the liver and the spleen, although there was a notable correspondence between, on one hand, liver TILs and C1, and on the other, spleen TILs and C2 (Figure 5g–i).
evidence: This describes the tissue-specific distribution of CD8+ T cell clusters in PDX samples.

claim: Several TCR clones were unique to or overrepresented in the liver biopsies of mice with MART1-selected T cells, as compared to unselected TILs or spleen samples.
source: Investigating the TCR clonotypes represented in the four experimental conditions revealed several clones unique to or overrepresented in the liver biopsies of mice with MART1-selected T cells, as compared to unselected TILs or spleen samples (Figure 5j).
evidence: This describes TCR clonotype distribution across experimental conditions.

claim: TCR clones unique to or overrepresented in liver biopsies of mice with MART1-selected T cells are likely to be strongly enriched for TRLs.
source: Given that these clones have been sorted to enrich for reactivity toward an antigen known to be presented by UM22 cells, and that they have successfully migrated to the liver tumor, this subset is likely to be strongly enriched for TRLs.
evidence: This is an inference about TRL enrichment based on selection and migration patterns.

claim: Differential expression analysis between TRL subset and unselected TILs in PDX livers revealed TNFRFS9 (4-1BB) as a statistically significant marker.
source: Differential expression analysis between this TRL subset and unselected TILs found in the livers of PDX mice revealed statistically significant genes that may be potential markers of the tumor-reactive phenotype (Figure 5k, Figure 5—figure supplement 1j, Supplementary file 4). This included the activation marker TNFRFS9 (4-1BB) as well as KIR2DL4, which has been found to be expressed in certain exhausted subsets of CD8+ T cells (Figure 2c; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes results of differential expression analysis identifying TRL markers.

claim: KIR2DL4 was identified as a statistically significant marker of TRLs and has been found to be expressed in certain exhausted subsets of CD8+ T cells.
source: Differential expression analysis between this TRL subset and unselected TILs found in the livers of PDX mice revealed statistically significant genes that may be potential markers of the tumor-reactive phenotype (Figure 5k, Figure 5—figure supplement 1j, Supplementary file 4). This included the activation marker TNFRFS9 (4-1BB) as well as KIR2DL4, which has been found to be expressed in certain exhausted subsets of CD8+ T cells (Figure 2c; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a marker identified through differential expression analysis with literature support.

claim: The TRL subset identified in PDX livers bears a striking resemblance to a recently described group of TIM-3+IL7R- tumor-reactive tissue-resident memory cells in lung cancer, characterized by expression of KRT86, DUSP4, and LAYN.
source: Interestingly, this subset also bears a striking resemblance to a recently described group of TIM-3+IL7R- tumor-reactive tissue-resident memory cells in lung cancer, further characterized by the specific expression of KRT86, DUSP4, and LAYN (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Clarke et al., 2019).
evidence: This draws a comparison to a previously described cell type supported by a citation.

claim: The TIM-3+IL7R-KRT86+DUSP4+LAYN+ cell subset was enriched in patients responding to anti-PD1 therapy in lung cancer.
source: This set was enriched in patients responding to anti-PD1 therapy (Clarke et al., 2019).
evidence: This references findings from a previous study about treatment response.

claim: Cells expressing the KRT86+DUSP4+LAYN+ marker combination were present in biopsy samples, predominantly in exhausted clusters.
source: Cells expressing this marker combination were also present in biopsy samples, predominantly in exhausted clusters (Figure 5l and m), as well as in TIL cultures from UM22 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This describes the presence and distribution of cells with specific markers in biopsies.

claim: Cells expressing the KRT86+DUSP4+LAYN+ marker combination were present in TIL cultures from UM22.
source: Cells expressing this marker combination were also present in biopsy samples, predominantly in exhausted clusters (Figure 5l and m), as well as in TIL cultures from UM22 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This describes the presence of cells with specific markers in TIL cultures.

claim: The KRT86+DUSP4+LAYN+ marker combination might suggest avenues for enriching TRLs from biopsies for use with ex vivo expansion and ACT.
source: This might suggest avenues for enriching TRLs from biopsies for use with ex vivo expansion and ACT based on their gene expression profiles.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications based on marker identification.

claim: In the UM22 liver metastasis model, T cells were pushed out of the tumor.
source: In the UM22 liver metastasis model, we found evidence that T cells were pushed out of the tumor.
evidence: This describes an observation from the PDX experiment.

claim: T cell exclusion in UM22 may partly explain the failure of immune checkpoint inhibitors in many patients with UM.
source: This may partly explain the failure of immune checkpoint inhibitors in many patients (Algazi et al., 2016) and why ACT with TILs does not work for the majority of patients with metastatic UM (Chandran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental observation to clinical outcomes.

claim: T cell exclusion in UM22 may partly explain why ACT with TILs does not work for the majority of patients with metastatic UM.
source: This may partly explain the failure of immune checkpoint inhibitors in many patients (Algazi et al., 2016) and why ACT with TILs does not work for the majority of patients with metastatic UM (Chandran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental observation to clinical outcomes.

claim: TRLs that preferentially migrated to liver metastases in mice appeared to resemble a recently described IL7R-HAVCR2+KRT86+DUSP4+LAYN+ subset associated with response to anti-PD1 therapy in lung cancer.
source: We identified marker genes and phenotypic states that might be used to identify relevant subsets present in patient biopsies and TIL cultures. These T cells appeared to resemble a recently described IL7R-HAVCR2+KRT86+DUSP4+LAYN+ subset, which has been associated with response to anti-PD1 therapy in lung cancer (Clarke et al., 2019).
evidence: This draws a comparison between identified TRLs and a previously described cell type.

claim: TRLs that preferentially migrated to liver metastases tended to express ITGAE (CD103), suggesting they may be tissue-resident memory cells.
source: They also tended to express ITGAE (CD103), suggesting that they may be tissue-resident memory cells.
evidence: This describes marker expression and provides an interpretation about cell type.

claim: The IL7R-HAVCR2+KRT86+DUSP4+LAYN+ subset was identified in PDX liver metastases, cultured TILs, and patient biopsies.
source: This subset was identified in both PDX liver metastases, cultured TILs, and patient biopsies.
evidence: This describes the presence of a specific cell subset across different sample types.

claim: The phenotypes of cells with the IL7R-HAVCR2+KRT86+DUSP4+LAYN+ marker combination were predominantly exhaustion-like in PDX samples and biopsies.
source: The phenotypes of cells with this marker combination were predominantly exhaustion-like in the PDX samples as well as in biopsies.
evidence: This describes the phenotypic characteristics of cells with specific markers.

claim: Mapping of experimentally identified MART1-reactive T cells back to biopsies and computational prediction of tumor antigen-recognizing T cells suggested an overrepresentation of TRL candidates in exhausted and late-activated gene expression-based clusters.
source: This is compatible with the results from the profiling of biopsy CD8+ T cells, where mapping of experimentally identified MART1-reactive T cells back to biopsies and computational prediction of tumor antigen-recognizing T cells suggested an overrepresentation of TRL candidates in exhausted and late-activated gene expression-based clusters.
evidence: This summarizes findings from multiple analytical approaches.

claim: Whether cells expressing canonical exhaustion-related markers are truly dysfunctional or capable of eliciting an antitumor response remains to be explored.
source: Whether cells expressing these canonical exhaustion-related markers are truly dysfunctional or capable of eliciting an antitumor response remains to be explored (Clarke et al., 2019).
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the functional status of exhausted T cells.

claim: In the UM1 liver metastasis model, the tumor was eradicated by TILs.
source: In the UM1 liver metastasis model, the tumor was eradicated, demonstrating that TILs can cause a complete response also of liver metastases.
evidence: This describes experimental results showing tumor eradication.

claim: TILs can cause a complete response of liver metastases in UM.
source: In the UM1 liver metastasis model, the tumor was eradicated, demonstrating that TILs can cause a complete response also of liver metastases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the UM1 PDX experiment.

claim: Single-cell data from the UM1 liver metastasis model confirmed the loss of melanoma cells after TIL treatment.
source: The single-cell data obtained confirmed the loss of melanoma cells but it also resulted in a loss of CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This describes single-cell sequencing results after tumor eradication.

claim: Single-cell data from the UM1 liver metastasis model showed a loss of CD8+ T cells after tumor eradication.
source: The single-cell data obtained confirmed the loss of melanoma cells but it also resulted in a loss of CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This describes single-cell sequencing results after tumor eradication.

claim: The fate of CD8 T cells after an acute immunological reaction is either death of the effector cells or development of memory.
source: It is well known in immunology that the fate of CD8 T cells after an acute immunological reaction is either death of the effector cells or development of memory.
evidence: This is a statement of established immunological knowledge.

claim: Analysis of CD4+ T cells of the same clonotype in liver versus spleen suggested that some level of activation/exhaustion remained even after tumor clearance.
source: This analysis did indeed suggest that some level of activation/exhaustion remained even after tumor clearance.
evidence: This describes results of differential expression analysis between tissues.

claim: Some TCRs from the co-culture experiment designed to reveal TRLs were identified in vivo among the CD8 and proliferative cells in the UM1 model.
source: Moreover, some of the TCRs from the co-culture experiment of tumorspheres and TILs designed to reveal TRLs were indeed identified in vivo among the CD8 and the proliferative cells.
evidence: This describes overlap between in vitro and in vivo identified TRLs.

claim: PDX models such as UM22 and UM1 will be useful in future studies where T cells are sorted for potential markers prior to expansion or infusion.
source: We are therefore confident that PDX models such as UM22 and UM1 will be useful in future studies where T cells are sorted for potential markers prior to expansion or infusion, where the T cells are genetically engineered or grown in cocktails of factors to enhance potency and stemness.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the developed models for future research.

claim: The PDX model is appropriate for further humanization to unravel the interplay between tumor cells, liver cells and stroma cells, myeloid cells, and other immune cells.
source: We also propose the model to be appropriate for further humanization to unravel the interplay between tumor cells, liver cells and stroma cells, myeloid cells, and other immune cells.
evidence: This is a proposal for future applications of the PDX model.

claim: TCRs that recognize different antigens can share CDR3β chains.
source: Importantly, TCRs that recognize different antigens can share CDR3β chains.
evidence: This is a statement about TCR biology and database limitations.

claim: The TCR alpha chain is more promiscuous than the beta chain but not always reported in TCR databases.
source: The TCR alpha chain is even more promiscuous but not always reported in these databases, which makes it difficult to find accurate TCR pair matches.
evidence: This describes limitations of current TCR databases.

claim: An increasing body of literature suggests that bystander cells in tumors are often antigen-experienced and can be directed against bacteria or viruses.
source: Nevertheless, an increasing body of literature suggests that bystander cells in tumors are often antigen-experienced, can be directed against bacteria or viruses, and even participate in tumor control, for instance during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy (Rosato et al., 2019; Çuburu et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2022).
evidence: This summarizes findings from multiple studies about bystander T cells.

claim: Bystander T cells can participate in tumor control during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy.
source: Nevertheless, an increasing body of literature suggests that bystander cells in tumors are often antigen-experienced, can be directed against bacteria or viruses, and even participate in tumor control, for instance during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy (Rosato et al., 2019; Çuburu et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes a role for bystander T cells supported by citations.

claim: Whether the presence of foreign antigen-specific T cells is beneficial for cellular immunotherapy remains to be evaluated.
source: Whether the presence of foreign antigen-specific T cells is beneficial for cellular immunotherapy remains to be evaluated.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the role of bystander T cells in immunotherapy.

claim: The study profiled the tumor microenvironment of metastatic UM and identified the phenotypes of tumor-reactive T cell subsets.
source: In summary, we profiled the tumor microenvironment of metastatic UM and identified the phenotypes of tumor-reactive T cell subsets.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's main findings.

claim: The results provide new avenues for targeted expansion of T cells to improve cellular and immune checkpoint immunotherapy.
source: The results of this study provide new avenues for targeted expansion of T cells to improve cellular and immune checkpoint immunotherapy.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the study findings.

claim: To potentiate TIL therapies in UM, immune cold tumors likely need to be turned hot to create an inflammatory environment promoting T cell infiltration.
source: Importantly, however, to potentiate TIL therapies in UM, immune cold tumors likely need to be turned hot, i.e., to create an inflammatory environment promoting T cell infiltration.
evidence: This is a speculation about requirements for improving TIL therapy.

claim: Lymphodepletion is needed to avoid existing T cells sequestering IL2 needed for the TIL infusion product.
source: Simultaneously, lymphodepletion is needed to avoid existing T cells sequestering IL2 needed for the TIL infusion product.
evidence: This is a statement about requirements for TIL therapy based on immunological principles.

claim: Tumor-targeting treatments such as IHP or percutaneous hepatic perfusion may fulfill the needs of creating an inflammatory environment and lymphodepletion.
source: Tumor-targeting treatments such as IHP or percutaneous hepatic perfusion may fulfill these needs and could act as adjuvant therapy for both immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment and TIL therapy.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential combination therapies.

claim: Melphalan triggers immunogenic death, which may lead to influx of new T cells into cold tumors.
source: As melphalan triggers immunogenic death, influx of new T cells into cold tumors may occur, partly explaining the very high response rate of these therapies (Olofsson Bagge et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of action of melphalan-based therapies.

claim: Ongoing clinical trials are combining locoregional therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors.
source: Ongoing clinical trials are combining locoregional therapy with ICI (NCT04463368) to capitalize on this concept.
evidence: This describes ongoing clinical research.

claim: Combination of liver-directed therapy and TIL therapy is warranted in future animal experiments and clinical trials.
source: Combination of liver-directed therapy and TIL therapy is also warranted in future animal experiments and clinical trials.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research directions.

claim: PDX models are optimal to capture the intra-patient heterogeneity of cancer.
source: We propose that PDX models are optimal to capture the intra-patient heterogeneity of cancer and that multiple mechanisms in tumor immunology and treatment can be modeled at single-cell resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of PDX models based on the study's findings.

claim: Multiple mechanisms in tumor immunology and treatment can be modeled at single-cell resolution in PDX models.
source: We propose that PDX models are optimal to capture the intra-patient heterogeneity of cancer and that multiple mechanisms in tumor immunology and treatment can be modeled at single-cell resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of PDX models based on the study's approach.
